title: third-party-dependency-resilience-and-quarantine-runbook-2026
author: Maya Thompson
body:
Summary
This runbook describes how Redwood SRE handles reliability and capacity impacts caused by third-party dependencies (external model registries, cloud storage, telemetry ingest pipelines, downstream partner APIs, and managed database services). It defines SLO mapping for dependent systems, error-budget policy when third-party issues surface, capacity and timeout guardrails, and a standardized quarantine workflow to contain and recover from dependency-induced degradation.

Scope
- Applies to platform-facing services (Redwood API, Dedicated routing, Console ingestion, KV cache sync) that call or rely on external services.
- Not intended for purely internal downstream jobs that do not affect customer-facing SLOs (those have separate runbooks).

Definitions
- Dependent service: any external service (SaaS, managed cloud service, external partner API) that Redwood calls synchronously or asynchronously.
- Dependency SLO: the expected reliability contract we map a dependency to for the purposes of capacity/error-budgeting.
- Quarantine: an emergency state where traffic to a particular dependency is isolated, routed to fallback, or rate-limited to prevent system-wide failure.

Why this matters
Third-party outages frequently look like internal latency spikes, queue growth, or cascading OOMs. Without fast quarantine and well-defined fallbacks, a single degraded dependency can consume headroom and burn error budget across multiple services. This runbook reduces blast radius and preserves customer-facing SLOs.

Dependency SLO mapping (examples)
| Redwood surface | Observable metric | Mapped dependency SLO | Rationale |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Redwood API token generation | 99th p50 latency | 99.5% requests < 200 ms for token validation | auth provider latency via third party impacts token handshakes |
| Embedding pipeline | end-to-end success rate | 99.0% success for trained model-hosting calls | embedding failures degrade PLG onboarding UX |
| Console telemetry ingestion | ingestion success rate | 99.5% for daily batches | backpressure can cause size-based retention loss |

Error budget & containment policy
1) Assign an operational dependency severity when an incident is detected:
   - D1 (critical): dependency is failing and causing customer-visible SLO breaches or >X headroom consumption (see threshold table).
   - D2 (major): intermittent failures or latency that increases error budget burn but still under customer-visible threshold.
   - D3 (minor): low-rate anomalies; monitor.
2) On D1/D2 classification, SRE must:
   - Trigger quarantine evaluation within 10 minutes.
   - Reduce traffic to dependency by 50–90% depending on fallback maturity.
3) Error-budget crediting: when a dependency is confirmed out-of-scope (third-party incident), the owning SRE team may apply a proportional error-budget exemption to customer SLOs after post-incident review. The decision template is in the Post-incident section.

Thresholds & decision matrix
| Symptom | Immediate trigger | Quarantine action |
|---|---:|---|
| Upstream HTTP 5xx > 5% of requests for 3m | D1 | Route to cached responses or fast-failure mode (50–90% reduction) |
| P95 latency x2 baseline for 10m | D2 | Lower concurrency and enable circuit breaker (50% reduction) |
| Queue depth growth > 4x normal | D2 | Backpressure producers, enable sampling |

Capacity planning considerations for dependencies
- Reserve headroom: maintain a dependency-hedge pool equal to 15% of steady-state request capacity for at least the top 20% tenants by qps. This pool is used for graceful degradation fallback routes.
- Warm-up and shadowing: before integrating a new dependency, shadow traffic at 5–10% for 48–72 hours across typical tails and token lengths. Record tail latencies and cold-start variance.
- Throttles and rate windows: cap per-tenant concurrent calls to external dependencies (default 5) with exponential backoff and jitter. Document overrides in tenant profile for Dedicated customers.

Runbook: Immediate actions (first 30 minutes)
1) Detect: confirm alerts for dependency anomalies (5xx/latency/queue). Open an incident Slack channel and tag #sre-oncall.
2) Triage: identify the dependency, ingress path, and affected tenant scope. Use telemetry dashboards: dependency-tracing -> recent traces -> top causes.
3) Short-circuit: if D1, execute quarantine play (see CLI and examples). Steps:
   - Toggle circuit breaker: POST /api/control/circuit-breakers {"dependency":"<name>","state":"open"}
   - Apply traffic reroute: update routing rule to point to fallback pool, using the routing control API.
   - Update status page: note degraded external dependency.
4) Communicate: notify product and customer success with initial impact estimate and mitigation steps.

Runbook: triage and mitigation flow (30m–4h)
1) Root cause hypothesis: correlate deployment events, configuration changes, cert expiries, and cloud provider incidents.
2) Scale or reduce: if the dependency is slow but available, reduce internal concurrency and increase client-side timeouts to avoid build-up.
3) Engage partner: open support ticket with dependency provider using provided run template (include traces, request IDs, and sample curl commands). Keep ticket ID in incident channel.
4) Iterate: if fallback reduces customer impact and error budget consumption drops, keep quarantine until root cause confirmed or a workaround is in place.

Quarantine & rollback procedures
- Quarantine types:
   - Traffic redirection to internal cache or noop handler.
   - Fast fail (immediate 503 with explanatory payload).
   - Sampling (reduce to steady 1–5% for diagnostic calls).
- Rollback criteria:
   - Dependency's 5xx < baseline + 1% for 30 minutes and P95 latency back within 1.5x baseline.
   - Telemetry indicates no queue buildup and CPU/mem across affected services stable.
- Stepwise rollback: 25% -> 50% -> 100% over 15-minute intervals with monitoring at each step.

Tooling & telemetry requirements
- Required dashboards: dependency-health (per-dependency), headroom-consumption, queue-lengths, tail-latency by tenant.
- Traces: span tags must include dependency.name, dependency.request_id, and tenant.id.
- Synthetic tests: run per-minute lightweight health checks (smithy probes) for each external endpoint; maintain 7-day rolling baseline.
- Automation: quarantine actions must be scriptable via control-plane API and exposed to incident CLI: redwoodctl quarantine <dependency> --mode=fast-fail --percent=75

Ownership & escalation matrix
- Primary: runtime-infrastructure (pager rotation).
- Secondary: platform-integration (day rotation).
- Tertiary: on-call for product-engineering when feature flags or recent rollouts are implicated.
- Escalate to engineering director when incident > 3 hours and > 10% customers impacted.

Post-incident review & evidence checklist
- Confirm timeline: alert -> quarantine -> mitigation -> rollback.
- Attach artifacts: alert graphs, trace snippets, routing change diff, control-plane API commands used, dependency provider ticket IDs.
- Root-cause hypothesis: was it an external outage, capacity mismatch, config error, or cert/permission issue?
- Policy decision: determine whether customer SLOs receive an exemption or partial credit. Include the proportionality rationale.
- Remediation actions (owner + due date): e.g., increase headroom hedge to 20% (runtime-infra, 2025-07-15), add extra synthetic checks for dependency X (platform-integration, 2025-06-30).

Appendix A — sample quarantine CLI usage
# Fast-fail 80% of traffic to model-registry-prod
redwoodctl quarantine model-registry-prod --mode fast-fail --percent 80 --reason "external 5xx spike"

Appendix B — minimal JSON payload for control-plane circuit-breaker API
{
  "dependency": "model-registry-prod",
  "action": "open",
  "percent": "80",
  "initiator": "sre-oncall@redwood.com",
  "comment": "Fast-fail due to sustained 5xx > 5%"
}

Appendix C — Quarantine decision checklist (short)
1) Confirm customer-facing SLO impact and estimate error-budget burn.
2) Verify fallback available (cache, local model, noop).
3) Execute quarantine and monitor for 15 minutes.
4) Keep stakeholder comms updated every 30 minutes.
5) Prepare rollback plan before full restoration.
